notesStmt.note: The cancelled material on the reverse sides of this manuscript pertains to the printing of the "Sands at Seventy" supplement to Leaves of Grass that was bound into an issue of the book during the last months of 1888. The biographical draft on the front, therefore, dates to sometime between late 1888 and mid-1889, when the copy for Camden's Compliment went to the printer.

This autobiographical sketch appears to be an early draft of the "Autobiographic Note" that appeared in Camden's Compliment to Walt Whitman (Philadelphia: David McKay, 1889), edited by Horace Traubel. Whitman then incorporated the material, with additional minor revisions, into the longer essay "Some Personal and Old Age Jottings," for publication in Good-Bye My Fancy (1891).

Walt Whitman
‸ ‸Walt, poet, was born May 31, 1819, on his fathers at his parents' farm house, West Hills, western Suffolk County, Long Island, New York State; of English stock
on from the father's side, and on from
that of the mother (Louisa Van Velsor) of Holland Dutch. The family moved to Brooklyn early; and in that place, and in New York City, W. W's boyhood and early manhood passed. He went to the public schools, and in due time learned the printer's trade, and worked at it. He p u also lived in the country, ‸Long Island, taught school, labored at farm⹀toil and house⹀building, and published a weekly newspaper. New York and Brooklyn, however, were his principal headquarters till nearly 30 years of age, when he started traveling, first to Louisiana, for passing a year there,, and then to leisurely visits and occupation, in nearly all the Southern and Western States, one after the other. Then returning to Brooklyn, he put in shape and issued (1855) the first portion of Leaves of Grass, which has been fashioned and increased until now (1888) is is considered finished, by the author's last pieces, Sands at Seventy, as annex to the previous ones.

During 1862 to 1865 ‸inclusive W W was ‸was arduously occupied in the area of the Civil War in Maryland and Virginia, and in ‸ and around Washington City, absorbed with the wounded and sick of the armies, both northern and southern; giving ‸fully three years with to those special ministerings. He had always always been of possessed the best health and strength, but soon about the close of the contest, he was prostrated ‸by a severe stroke of paralysis. Though he surmount-

it, a broken physique remained,resulted, and some six attacks have at times resulted followed from it since. His literary works are comprehended under three titles, his the Leaves of Grass, his his main work and form of poetic expression, and his main work, passing through five stages or increments, beginning in 1855 and completed in 1888; his prose book, Specimen Days and Coll Collect, issued 1883, forming biographical notes, memoranda of personal memoranda during the Civil War, with various essays, including Democratic Vistas; and lastly a smaller work November Boughs, of poems and prose.

He has never recovered from the physical paralysis of the war-period and agitation of 1855 to 1860 to 1865, ‸ but ‸his mental powers remaining unaffected, he has steadily worked at his literary plans and induring 1888, at in his 70th year, finished his the booklet of November Boughs, his last work.
